title: Novenas
hook: nine days of prayer, after the apostles waiting for the Spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sacred Heart at home: an image where the family really lives, and a guest invited to supper. Your line was he lives here. Who was at your table? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

What would you keep doing for nine days straight, for someone else? A woman's brother is having surgery next week. Her aunt hands her a folded leaflet: a short prayer, the same each day, nine days of it. Start tonight, the aunt says, and you'll finish before he goes in. The woman has never done anything like it, and she isn't sure what it will do. But nine days is something she can hold in her hands. Today's word is the name for that.
screen: `NINE DAYS, FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` → `A FOLDED LEAFLET.` → `START TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: A novena is nine days of prayer, for one intention or to prepare for a feast. The prayer itself can be short: a few lines, the same each day, or a new reflection each day. What makes it a novena is the shape: nine days, kept one after another. Where does that shape come from? Tradition points to the apostles. In Acts, before he ascends, Jesus tells them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the promise of the Father. So they wait, and pray, and the Spirit comes at Pentecost. Tradition counts that waiting as nine days and calls it the first novena. That's tomorrow's story, so we'll leave them in the upper room for now. Next, the kinds. Some novenas prepare for a feast, like Christmas or a saint's day. Some ask for something: work, healing, a safe birth. Some are for the dead, praying for someone who has just died. Some are said to a saint, asking that saint to pray alongside the one who asks. Third, what a novena is not. It isn't a vending machine: nine coins in, one answer out. Some leaflets promise that a certain novena never fails. The Church doesn't teach that; the Catechism warns against treating any prayer as if its power came from saying it correctly. Jesus says in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "And when you are praying, speak not much, as the heathens. For they think that in their much speaking they may be heard." A novena isn't about piling up words. Last, what it actually does. It brings a person back to the same intention day after day, long after the first rush of worry has faded. Day one is easy. Day six, when nothing seems to be happening, may be where the real praying starts. Nine days is practice in waiting, the way the apostles waited, without knowing when or how the answer will come.
screen: `NINE DAYS, ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `FOR FEASTS, NEEDS, THE DEAD.` · `NOT A VENDING MACHINE.` · `PRACTICE IN WAITING.` · then, large: `WAIT FOR THE PROMISE OF THE FATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: start a nine-day prayer, today. Close your eyes, if that helps. Bring to mind one person or one need that's been weighing on you lately. Name it simply, in a few words. That's your intention. If you pray, you can choose a prayer you already know, the Our Father or the Hail Mary, and say it once a day for that intention, for nine days, beginning now. If you don't pray, you can still keep the shape: one minute a day, for nine days, of holding that person in mind. Say the intention once, quietly. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Novena. Nine days of prayer, kept one after another, for an intention or before a feast. Tradition traces the shape to the apostles waiting for the Spirit. Today's word.
Your line: nine days. Today, write your intention and today's date somewhere you'll see it tomorrow, so day two has a place to begin. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics pray novenas, nine consecutive days of prayer, before feasts such as Christmas, for particular needs, for the dead, or asking a saint's intercession; parishes sometimes hold public novenas with a prayer service each evening.

fork.setup: a leaflet says its novena never fails, as long as you don't skip a word. what does Catholic teaching say?
options: it's true, if every word is said.
prayer's power doesn't come from saying it correctly.

fork.reveal: the Catechism warns against treating prayer as if its power lay in correct repetition, and Jesus says not to speak much, as if many words would be heard.

trapdoor: what you thought: a novena is a prayer that works if you say it nine times.
what it means: nine days of returning to one intention, or preparing for a feast, shaped like the apostles' waiting for the Spirit.
what a scholar hears: CCC 2111 calls it superstition to credit a prayer's power to its mere outward performance; the count of nine is tradition's reading of the wait in Acts, which gives no number.

sources.quoted: And when you are praying, speak not much, as the heathens. For they think that in their much speaking they may be heard.

notes: Acts does not count the days between the Ascension and Pentecost as nine; the script attributes the count and 'the first novena' to tradition. Acts 1:4 ('wait for the promise of the Father') is paraphrased, with the phrase used on screen.
CCC 2111 (superstition includes attributing the efficacy of prayers or sacramental signs to their mere external performance) paraphrased.
Trapdoor: the novendiales (nine days of Masses/mourning after a pope's death, per Universi Dominici Gregis) offered as a parallel nine-day pattern; confirm wording.
'Some leaflets promise that a certain novena never fails' describes popular leaflets, not Church teaching; confirm the framing is fair and not dismissive of those who pray them.
